strengths: Converting forest and ReLU partitions into class-conditional Gaussian mixtures is an understandable construction with an identifiable audience in density estimation and uncertainty estimation.

The five controlled two-dimensional simulations provide useful illustrations of extrapolation behavior. Figure 2 reports 45 repetitions with interquartile bands, and Table 1 reports substantial OOD AUROC improvements over the parent models, reaching 0.97–0.99.

The human study adds an interesting behavioral perspective and reports its participant exclusions transparently. Posterior visualizations, main-text pseudocode, and a public code link help communicate the approach.
weaknesses: Necessary—repair or withdraw the theoretical claims. Theorem 1 incorrectly assumes that a shrinking Gaussian becomes uniform over its polytope. For uniform data in a one-dimensional cell of width h, the population moment-fitted Gaussian has variance h²/12, giving h K(center) = sqrt(6/pi), approximately 1.382, although the target uniform density is 1. Shrinking the cell does not eliminate this discrepancy. The binomial treatment of counts in partitions learned from the same data and the disappearance of covariance terms also require justification. Moreover, asymptotic unbiasedness alone does not establish the introduction's convergence claim, and no comparative efficiency result supports the abstract.

Necessary—qualify the OOD and generative interpretation. For a fixed fitted model, Equations 3.6–3.8 approach the empirical class prior as inputs become arbitrarily distant; this is uniform only for balanced priors. Gaussian tail decay does not establish the desired behavior throughout every distribution with disjoint support, particularly near the training support. Also, adding a positive constant to a density on R^d gives an infinite integral. The unshifted Gaussian mixtures are valid densities, but the shifted quantities require interpretation as posterior regularization or replacement with a proper background model. Limit the robustness claims to what is demonstrated; reported FPR@95 values remain approximately 0.28–0.41.

Necessary—reconcile the performance claims with Figure 2. The abstract claims that the generative models outperform their parents at small sample sizes, while Section 5.2 claims consistently better posterior estimates and the conclusion claims no loss of in-distribution performance. Figure 2 contains clear counterexamples: KDN has substantially larger Gaussian XOR Hellinger distance than DN at small sample sizes, and both kernel variants have higher Circle classification error than their parents in that regime. Describe the observed tradeoffs instead of claiming general dominance.

Necessary—make the implemented method and evaluation reproducible. Equation 3.4 compares preactivations, whereas Algorithm 3 accumulates postactivation differences; these define different weights, already for a single hidden layer. The manuscript omits values or selection procedures for h, T, and C, and does not specify covariance regularization despite potentially singular estimates in sparsely populated polytopes. Clarify training, validation, and test sampling; correct the Gaussian XOR definition, which currently assigns identical mixtures to both classes; and resolve the inconsistent description of FPR@95 as a false-negative versus false-positive rate.

Necessary—support or narrow the human-likeness claim. Figure 3 compares humans with RF and DN, without directly evaluating KDF or KDN agreement with human responses. The highlighted 82-degree slice lacks a selection rationale and uncertainty estimates. Furthermore, an average class probability near 0.5 can arise from opposing confident responses, so it does not establish low individual confidence. Analyze individual confidence and quantitative model–human agreement, or present these observations as exploratory motivation.

Optional improvements: Compare with ordinary KDE or Gaussian mixtures using the same bias rule, and ablate neighborhood weighting and the bias to identify the source of the gains. Higher-dimensional experiments and computational measurements would extend the findings. A carefully supported low-dimensional study is sufficient in scope for TMLR; the rejection recommendation rests on the substantive correctness and evidential problems above.
